newsitem.title: UK: BOE plans '97 money market reform in line with EU.
newsitem.headline: BOE plans '97 money market reform in line with EU.

text.p: The Bank of England on Wednesday announced plans to shake up its archaic money markets early in 1997 and bring them more into line with their counterparts elsewhere in the European Union.

In a series of sweeping new proposals, the Bank is to widen the group of assets used in its daily money market operations to include gilt repurchase (repo) transactions, and greatly enlarge the list of counterparties allowed to participate.

The Bank said the changes would make its operations similar to those now being discussed by the European Monetary Institute (EMI) -- the forerunner of the European Central Bank which will set monetary policy after economic and monetary union in 1999.

"The changes are consistent with the direction and spirit of proposals under discussion at the EMI for future monetary operations in euro, which are of relevance whether or not the UK participates in monetary union," it said in a statement.
But Bank officials quickly distanced themselves from suggestions that the prospect of a single European currency was behind the proposed changes to money market operations.
"Bringing UK operations into line with those being discussed by the EMI was not the main motive in introducing these changes," said Ian Plenderleith, executive director at the Bank.

The Bank of England's unique method of providing liquidity to Britain's money market involves buying bills at set rates from discount houses, which are "middlemen" between the central bank and UK clearing banks.
In expanding the group of participants to include banks, building societies and securities firms, the discount houses will soon find a chunk of their traditional business has disappeared.
But discount house officials put a brave face on the changes. The chairman of one discount house, Cater Allen, said his firm should actually benefit from the changes.

"Our money market subsidiary Cater Allen Limited already holds a leading position in the gilt repo market. We believe we will benefit from the introduction of the Bank as a major daily user," said James Barclay.
Philip Shaw, group economist at another, Union Plc, agreed discount houses need not suffer too much under the new system.
"Most have diversified their business considerably in recent years. And these proposals come as no surprise. We have been expecting these changes for a few years now."

Using the gilt repo as a tool to provide liquidity would also be seen by some as a first step towards more radical reform of Britain's money market and the way the central bank sets official interest rates.
But analysts said should Britain sign up to a single currency in 1999 or afterwards, the Bank would almost certainly have to make other key changes to its money market operations.

Most signficantly, the system of banks' balancing their accounts with the Bank of England at the end of each day would need to be replaced by a minimum reserve system averaged over a month or so, similar to the present German system, they said.
